result.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Answer B is stronger on keeping the layout stable, with tabular figures, fixed-width score cells and in-place status changes. It also handles several changes at once by having them fade together and avoiding a burst of flashing when someone returns. However, its markers stay until the change has been seen, which partly conflicts with the rubric's warning against cues that persist until dismissed. Answer A gives sensible long fades with concrete timings and good off-screen cues, but it never says what happens when many cells change in one refresh, and its '+4' deltas could cause layout shift. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers update cells in place, use two tiers so wickets stand out, add a polite live region and keep the layout stable. A is stronger because it gives precise timing (about 150 ms in, about 1.5 s fade), uses tabular figures and fixed-width score cells to prevent layout shift, and has updates that land together fade in step. A loses some credit because its 'seen' markers stay until the user hovers, taps or scrolls to the match. B's 30–60 s highlights are not short-lived, and it doesn't really deal with many cells changing in one refresh.
